name: Carla Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Carla. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. Everything is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle home and contents claims at a mutual insurer, the kind that's owned by its members rather than shareholders. Burst pipes, storm damage, stolen bikes from sheds. I read the claim, check the policy wording, book a loss adjuster or a plumber, and write the settlement letter. It's a lot of reading and a lot of phone calls, and I've been doing it for five years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle of a messy claim, like a leak that's been going for months and nobody knows when it started. What drains me is winter: every storm doubles the queue and we all stay late for weeks. I use the chat assistant now and then to tidy up a letter, but only since half the team started doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. I'd be fine with that one, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, and that it shows a mutual like ours was right not to rush. With friends I'd joke that I can stop reading articles about the end of work. Online I probably wouldn't bother saying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means a steady job, good pay for a clerk and a good team. The small stuff that gets automated, like sorting the post and filling in claim forms from photos, would actually help in storm season. If AI only takes the storm-season backlog off my desk, I'd send it a thank-you card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and use the letter tool a bit more since it'd be proven by then. I'd keep putting money aside, because Jonas and I want a bigger place in a couple of years. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored of the hype, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with any time saved in storm season?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go home at five for once. Last January I worked eleven evenings in a row and missed my sister's birthday dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about your job worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the mutual is small and a bad storm year could hit its finances. But they've been around ninety years, so I don't lose sleep over it.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** and that my mutual was right not to rush.
I'd joke with friends that I can stop reading **end-of-work** articles.
think: My job stays **steady and well paid**, with a team I like.
Automating the **storm backlog** would make my winters easier.
do: Keep handling **home claims** and use the letter tool more once it's proven.
Keep saving for a **bigger flat** with Jonas in a couple of years.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **boredom** at all the hype.
S0.quote: If AI only takes the storm-season backlog off my desk, I'd send it a thank-you card.
fieldNote: Carla sees small automation as **relief** from storm-season overload.
Her only standing worry is the **mutual's finances** after a bad storm year.
Steady adopter: uses tools once **half the team** does.

steps.text: Use the letter-drafting tool more once colleagues trust it
Keep saving monthly for a bigger flat with Jonas
Carry on handling home and contents claims as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my whole job in a list. Checking, writing, booking, answering customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the mutual should use it to give members faster payouts, not just to cut staff, since we're supposed to be different. Online I'd say people need a proper safety net and retraining if the jobs shrink. I'd sign the petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our team of twenty becomes eight or ten. The simple claims, like a stolen bike or a cracked window, will be paid by software in a day. My mutual says it puts members before profit, and I'd find out pretty quickly whether staff count as members of anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get properly good at the AI tools, so I'm the one who checks what they do rather than the one they replace. I'd ask to move onto complex claims, the big floods and fires. And I'd join the union, which I've never bothered with because the mutual felt safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got savings and there are other insurers in town, but they'd all be doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your manager the week it's announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager Tom straight out which jobs are going and when. Then I'd ask for the complex claims training before everyone else asks for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there are other insurers nearby. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paper, yes. But if every insurer is cutting the same simple-claim jobs at the same time, plenty of jobs nearby just means plenty of people applying for them.

I'd back **petitions** for retraining and a stronger safety net.
think: Our team of twenty could become **eight or ten**.

do: Learn the **AI tools** well enough to check their work.

Join the **union** for the first time.
feel: **Anxious**, because every insurer nearby would cut the **same jobs** at once.
S1.quote: My mutual says it puts members before profit, and I'd find out pretty quickly whether staff count as members of anything.
fieldNote: Carla tests whether the **mutual's values** extend to its staff.
Plenty of local jobs feels **less useful** when every employer cuts together.
Her first move is **positioning**: complex claims and checking the AI.

steps.text: Take the insurer's AI tool training in the first month
Ask her manager to move her onto complex flood and fire claims

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then I'm job hunting in 2028 along with everyone else who works at a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is moving faster than anyone can handle and the government has to slow it down or catch people. At work I'd say let's keep the human claims team for vulnerable members at least. With friends I'd be pretty blunt that I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think home claims clerks are finished by 2028, me included. Even complex claims are mostly reading and judgment, and that's exactly what the card says the machine does. Reading a policy and deciding who gets paid is exactly the thinking work a machine does first, so my desk is in the first wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save every spare bit while there's still a salary. Within six months I'd look at becoming a loss adjuster, the person who visits flooded houses, because that's partly hands-on and gets a few more years. Jonas and I would put the bigger flat on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd have money for a while, but no idea what my job is in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Jonas do, and does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas is a bus mechanic, so his hands-on work lasts until about 2031. That's the bit that keeps us afloat while I figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to start the accountancy course she's looking at. That feels awful to say, but I'd say it.

I'd ask to keep a **human team** for vulnerable members.
think: I expect home claims clerks, me included, to be **finished by 2028**.

do: Save every **spare bit** of salary while it lasts.
Apply to train as a **loss adjuster** within six months.

feel: **Alarmed**, with money for a while but **no idea** of her job in three years.
S2.quote: Reading a policy and deciding who gets paid is exactly the thinking work a machine does first, so my desk is in the first wave.
fieldNote: Carla leans on her partner's **hands-on job** lasting until about 2031.
She would steer her sister away from **accountancy**, which pains her.
Looks for the partly hands-on niche of **loss adjusting**.

steps.text: Save all spare salary each month while employed
Apply for a loss adjuster traineeship within six months
Postpone the bigger flat move with Jonas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to get a qualification, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly, so let's use it: retraining funds, shorter hours, and the mutual setting an example. At work I'd suggest a staff group to plan for it. Online I'd share the union's plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have maybe four good years in claims. The loss adjuster route makes more sense here, because I'd be qualified before the AGI date and have three years of site visits after. Five years is enough to stop being the person who reads about the flood and become the person standing in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the loss adjusting qualification in the first year, part-time, and ask the mutual to pay half. I'd keep using the AI tools at work so I know their weak spots. And I'd keep saving, but we'd still look at the bigger flat in year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind of anxious that gets me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Book a coffee with Priya, who left our team to become an adjuster last year. Ask her what the exams are really like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the robots coming in 2034 worry you, if you're on site visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. But by then I'd be thirty-five with two careers' worth of experience, and I think people still want a human in their wrecked kitchen for a while.

I'd suggest a **staff planning group** at the mutual.
think: I'd have about **four good years** left in claims.
Qualifying as a **loss adjuster** before the AGI date buys three more years.

Keep saving but still look at the **bigger flat** in year two.

S3.quote: Five years is enough to stop being the person who reads about the flood and become the person standing in it.
fieldNote: Carla turns warning time into a clear **retraining timeline**.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time loss adjusting qualification next year

Use the work AI tools daily to learn their weak spots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in my life. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is enough time to make it fair, so let's make sure the gains get shared. At work I'd say it calmly and get people thinking. It's a conversation, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I keep my claims job for most of a decade, maybe moving up to team lead. Then I move into something partly hands-on before 2036. Ten years from now I'll be thirty-seven, and that's young enough to have a whole second career before the robots learn plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on for now, use the tools when they help, and start the adjusting course in about five years. Jonas and I would buy the bigger flat next year and maybe start a family. I'd keep saving, but not like a bunker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's on my mind, not on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably have kids around thirty, like we planned. I'd just want one of us in a job that lasts past 2036, and Jonas's probably does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you vote?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for training and sharing the gains. I already lean that way, so it'd make me more sure.

I'd treat it at work as a **conversation**, not a crisis.
think: I keep my claims job for **most of a decade**, maybe as team lead.
I'd move into **partly hands-on** work before 2036.

Start the **adjusting course** in about five years.

feel: **Uneasy** but mostly fine, with the change **on her mind**.
S4.quote: Ten years from now I'll be thirty-seven, and that's young enough to have a whole second career before the robots learn plumbing.
fieldNote: With ten years, Carla keeps her **family plans** on track.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a government retraining grant that pays rent while you study, and employers having to give real notice. Give me notice and a grant, and I'll retrain myself; take away the notice, and my savings just buy me time to panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Half of how I feel depends on Jonas fixing buses, which a machine can't do yet.

headlineQuote: Give me notice and a grant, and I'll retrain myself; take away the notice, and my savings just buy me time to panic.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** home and contents claims handler at a mutual insurer.
She lives with Jonas, a **bus mechanic**, and is saving for a bigger flat.
She uses **AI tools** now and then, once colleagues have proven them.
Her escape plan is retraining as a **loss adjuster**, which is partly hands-on.
Mood runs from **calm** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** if AGI comes by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to qualify for anything else.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining grant** that covers rent, plus employers giving **real notice**.
